opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the main reason is that GAMES 201 was recorded back in 2020, and a lot has changed since then, both in the field and in me.

At the time I was still a PhD student at MIT. We'd just released Taichi, and I put that course together pretty quickly. I was preparing slides late at night and lecturing live in Chinese to a huge online audience. I'm really grateful so many people watched it, and I still get messages from students who say it got them into physical simulation. But when I look back at those videos, I see a lot I'd do differently. Some explanations were rushed. Some derivations skipped steps that I now realize are exactly where beginners get stuck. And some of the code examples rely on Taichi APIs that have since evolved, so people trying to follow along today run into friction.

There's also a broader motivation. Physical simulation used to feel like a niche corner of computer graphics. Now it matters for robotics, for embodied AI, for differentiable physics, and for generating training data for learning systems. Many more people need to understand things like the material point method, finite elements, or fluid solvers, and many of them don't come from a graphics background. So I want a version that's more self-contained and more carefully structured, something that teaches the intuition first and then the math and the code.

And on a personal level, after a few years of building a company and thinking about tools, I've come to believe that good education is one of the highest-leverage things you can do. A well-made lecture can keep helping people for ten years. So if I'm going to put my name on something that lasts, I want it to be the best version I can make. That's really what the remaster is about.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions a large audience and students who benefited, but does not attribute the lectures’ favorable reception to a lack of simulation tutorials in China.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the course was put together quickly and that some explanations were rushed and derivations skipped steps, linking limited preparation time to insufficient technical detail.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the original Games 201 lectures were made in 2020, in a very different situation. I recorded them in a bit of a rush, honestly, during the pandemic, often late at night, and Taichi itself was still a young project back then. A lot of the APIs I demoed in those videos have since changed or been deprecated, so people who follow the lectures today sometimes copy the code, run it, and get errors. That is a frustrating experience, and it is not the fault of the learner.

The second reason is that my own understanding has grown. When I made the first version, I was still a PhD student, and I was explaining things like material point method, SPH, Eulerian fluid solvers, and so on mostly from the perspective of someone who had just implemented them. Since then I have spent years building a company around this kind of technology, talking with a lot of people in graphics, in robotics, in engineering, and I now have a clearer sense of which concepts actually matter, which ones confuse beginners, and where I skipped steps that I should not have skipped. I want to fix those gaps, give better intuition, and reorganize the sequence so it flows more naturally.

The third reason is the audience. Games 201 ended up reaching far more people than I expected. It was originally meant for a Chinese-speaking student audience, but now I get messages from people around the world who are learning physical simulation through it. So in the remastered edition I want to make it more accessible, with cleaner code, better visuals, and material that works for someone who is self-studying rather than attending a live course.

And finally, part of it is just that I enjoy teaching. Simulation is a beautiful subject. Watching a fluid or a piece of snow come alive on the screen from a hundred lines of code is still magical to me, and I want more people to feel that. The first version got people excited, and I think a remastered one can do that even better.

r001.rationale: The response says the lectures reached more people than expected and were originally for Chinese-speaking students, but it does not attribute their favorable reception to a lack of simulation tutorials in China.

r002.rationale: It mentions recording the lectures in a rush, but attributes skipped steps and gaps to the speaker’s then-limited experience and understanding, not to limited preparation time.

astra-6.text: I want to make the material more accessible and easier to follow. When you teach a course for the first time, you learn a lot about which ideas need more explanation and where the pacing could be better. A remastered edition is an opportunity to rethink that structure, improve the examples, and make the connection between the math and the code clearer. I’d like people to come away not just understanding the simulations they see, but feeling confident enough to build their own.
